title: Sowing tomatoes on a windowsill
summary: Eight seeds, one south-facing sill and a lesson in patience: how this year's tomatoes got started before the frost had gone.
body:
The frost is still on the shed roof most mornings, but the tomatoes cannot wait. They want ten weeks of growing before they go outside, so the first seeds go in now, indoors, on the warmest windowsill in the house.

## What I used

- A seed tray with a clear lid, washed since last year
- Peat-free seed compost, sieved to take out the lumps
- Eight seeds each of *Sungold* and *Black Krim*
- A plant label and a pencil — never a pen, which fades

## How it went

Fill the tray, firm it gently and water it **before** sowing, so the seeds are not washed into one corner. Press each seed a few millimetres down, cover it with a pinch of compost and put the lid on.

The Sungolds came up on day six. The Black Krims took eleven, by which time I had decided they were dead twice.

> A seedling that leans toward the glass is telling you something. Turn the tray a quarter every morning.

Once the first true leaves open — the jagged ones, not the smooth pair that come first — each seedling moves into its own pot.

title: A loaf for people in a hurry
summary: No starter, no kneading and no special tin — a weeknight loaf that is mostly waiting, and very little work.
body:
Sourdough is wonderful and I do not have the time for it on a Tuesday. This loaf asks for ten minutes of attention spread over an evening, and it is better than most bread you can buy.

## Ingredients

1. 500 g strong white flour
2. 10 g salt
3. 4 g instant yeast — a level teaspoon
4. 375 g lukewarm water

## Method

Stir everything together in a big bowl until there is no dry flour left. It will look rough and too wet; that is right. Cover it and leave it for half an hour.

Then, with a wet hand, lift one side of the dough and fold it over the rest. Turn the bowl and repeat four times. Do this three times, half an hour apart, and then leave it alone until it has doubled.

Tip it onto a floured tray, shape it gently into a round and bake at **230 °C** for 35 minutes, with a roasting tin of water on the shelf below for the first 15.

> Let it cool for an hour. Cutting a loaf while it is hot squashes the crumb, and nobody ever believes this until they try it.

title: Three days on the West Highland Way
summary: Rain, midges, one perfect evening at Inversnaid and what I would pack differently next time.
body:
We walked the middle section, from Drymen to Tyndrum, in three long days. It rained on two of them. I would go again tomorrow.

## Day one: Drymen to Rowardennan

Conic Hill is the first real climb, and the view from the top over Loch Lomond and its islands is the reason to start here. The path down the far side is steep and was, that morning, a stream.

## Day two: Rowardennan to Inverarnan

The loch-side path is slower than the map suggests: roots, rocks and short scrambles for most of the way. We stopped at Inversnaid for soup and watched the waterfall for far longer than we meant to.

## Day three: Inverarnan to Tyndrum

The glen opens out, the walking gets easier and the midges get worse.

## What I would change

- Two pairs of thin socks rather than one thick pair
- A head net. Laugh now.
- Less food — every village has a shop or a café
- Book the bunkhouse in Inverarnan well ahead

> The best hour of the trip was an unplanned one: sitting on a rock at Inversnaid, boots off, with the rain finally stopped.

title: The compost heap that finally worked
summary: Two years of a cold, wet, smelly heap — and the three changes that turned it into something worth spreading.
body:
For two years my compost heap was a slow, sour pile that smelled of old cabbage. This spring it got hot enough to steam. Here is what changed.

## More brown than you think

Kitchen scraps and grass clippings are *greens*: wet and full of nitrogen. Cardboard, dry leaves and straw are *browns*. I had been adding almost no browns at all. Now every caddy of scraps goes in with an armful of torn-up cardboard, roughly half and half by volume.

## Turn it

Once a fortnight I fork the whole heap into the empty bay next to it. Ten minutes, and it puts air back into the middle, where the work happens.

## Keep the rain off

An old piece of carpet over the top keeps the heap damp rather than soaking, and holds the warmth in.

> Squeeze a handful. It should feel like a wrung-out sponge: damp, but not dripping.

By October there should be a bay of dark, crumbly compost for the beds. I will report back.

title: Green sauce for everything
summary: What to do when the herb bed gets ahead of you: a sharp, salty green sauce that goes on almost anything.
body:
By June the parsley and mint have stopped asking permission. This sauce uses a lot of both, keeps for a week in the fridge and goes with grilled vegetables, eggs, fish, lamb and plain boiled potatoes.

## What goes in

- A big handful each of parsley, mint and basil
- A tablespoon of capers and two anchovies
- One small clove of garlic
- A teaspoon of Dijon mustard
- The juice of half a lemon
- Olive oil — about 100 ml

## How to make it

Chop the herbs, capers, anchovies and garlic together on a board until they are fine but not a paste. Scrape it all into a bowl, stir in the mustard and lemon, and add oil until it loosens into a sauce.

Taste it. It almost always needs more lemon.

> A knife gives a better sauce than a blender, which bruises the herbs and turns them dark.

title: A week of markets in southern Portugal
summary: Figs, sardines, piri-piri and a great deal of bread: what we ate, where we bought it and what came home in the suitcase.
body:
We rented a small flat in Olhão for a week and did almost nothing but go to markets and cook what we found.

## The fish market

Olhão's two red-brick market halls sit on the waterfront. One is fish: sardines, horse mackerel, octopus, clams, and things I could not name. Go before nine, when the boats have just come in and the stalls are at their best.

## The Saturday market

On Saturdays the growers from the hills set up outside, and this is where the fruit is. We lived on:

- Figs, green and purple, warm from the sun
- Tomatoes that tasted of something
- Small sweet melons, sold by smell
- Bread from a wood oven, sold by weight

## What came home

A jar of piri-piri oil, two tins of good sardines, a bag of dried figs and a cataplana, the copper clam-shaped pan, which has since been used exactly once.

> Ask the stallholder what to do with something you do not recognise. Every one of them will tell you, at length.

title: Keeping a garden notebook
summary: Why a few lines a week beat a perfect memory, and the five things worth writing down every time.
body:
Every spring I am sure I will remember when I sowed the beans, which variety did best and where the slugs were worst. I never do. So now there is a notebook, and these notes started in it.

## Five things to write down

1. **The date and the weather** — a cold week explains a lot later
2. **What went in, and where** — the variety, not just *beans*
3. **What came up**, and how many
4. **What went wrong** — pests, frost, forgetting to water
5. **What you would do differently**

## Keep it short

Three lines a week is plenty. A notebook you keep up beats a beautiful one you abandon in May.

> The most useful page I have is a list of the dates of the last frost, year by year. It is never the date the seed packet says.
